notes.meaning: Israel moved out from the pleasant oasis of Elim and entered the Desert of Sin. This happened on the fifteenth day of the second month, exactly one month after leaving Egypt. Their journey brought them into a harsh wasteland between Elim and Mount Sinai as their stored supplies were running out.

The entire assembly of Israel began to grumble loudly against Moses and Aaron. With their food gone, fear took over and their earlier songs of praise turned into open complaints. The discontent was not limited to a few people, but spread through the whole camp.

The people wished they had died back in Egypt rather than face hunger in the wilderness. They remembered their cruel slavery through rose-colored glasses, picturing pots full of meat and endless bread. In their panic, they falsely accused Moses of trying to starve the whole nation to death.

The Lord told Moses that He would rain bread down from heaven for the people. Each day the Israelites were to gather only what they needed for that single day. This daily supply was also a test to see whether they would trust God and follow His directions.

God explained that on the sixth day of the week, the people would bring home twice as much food as on ordinary days. When they prepared what they gathered, it would be double the normal daily amount. This extra supply would provide for them so they would not have to work the next day.

Moses and Aaron announced to the whole camp that evening would prove the Lord had rescued them from Egypt. The people had acted as if their human leaders had dragged them out on a whim. The coming food would show that God Himself was guiding and protecting them.

Moses promised that the next morning the people would see the Lord's glory revealed in His miraculous provision. God had heard their bitter complaints and chose to answer with mercy rather than anger. Moses reminded them that he and Aaron were merely servants, so the complaints were really aimed at God.

Moses made the promise plain: God would give meat in the evening and all the bread they needed in the morning. He stressed again that their complaints were not against human leaders, but against the Lord. Complaining about life's hardships is often a complaint against God's care.

Moses directed Aaron to summon the entire congregation to come near before the Lord. God had heard their grumbling and called them to stand before His presence. This gathered the people so they could witness God's response to their lack of faith.

As Aaron spoke to the assembly, the people looked out toward the wilderness. Suddenly, the glorious, shining presence of the Lord appeared in the cloud. This sudden flash of divine majesty warned the people to honor God and confirmed Moses' authority.

The Lord spoke to Moses from the glorious cloud, confirming that He had heard Israel's cries. He told Moses that they would eat meat at twilight and be filled with bread in the morning. This miracle was meant to lead them to know and trust Him as their God.

That evening, a huge flock of quail flew in and covered the campsite, providing plentiful meat. In the morning, a thick blanket of dew rested all around the camp. God fulfilled His promise swiftly by supplying both meat in the evening and the promise of bread by morning.

When the morning dew evaporated, thin white flakes remained on the desert ground, looking like hoarfrost. This clean, flaky food was completely unfamiliar to the people. It lay ready on the surface of the desert for them to gather.

The Israelites saw the strange flakes and asked one another what it was, since they had never seen anything like it. Moses told them that this was the very bread the Lord had provided for them to eat. God met their hunger in an unexpected, miraculous way.

The Lord commanded each person to gather as much food as was needed for his family. The standard measure was an omer, which was about two to three quarts per person in each tent. This ensured that every household had a fair and sufficient portion.

The people went out and gathered the flakes, some bringing in larger piles and some smaller ones. Yet when they measured it with an omer, those who gathered much had no extra, and those who gathered little had no shortage. God worked a miracle so that every family ended up with exactly what they needed to eat.

Moses instructed the people not to save any of the food until the next morning. They were to eat their daily portion and trust God to provide again when the new day arrived. God wanted them to live by daily faith rather than relying on stored food.

Some people refused to listen to Moses and hoarded food overnight. By morning, the stored food was crawling with worms and began to smell foul, which made Moses very angry. Their lack of trust led directly to rot and ruined food.

Every morning each family went out early and collected what they needed for the day. As the sun rose higher and the desert grew hot, whatever flakes remained on the ground melted away. This routine trained the people to seek God's provision promptly at the start of each day.

On the sixth day, the people gathered twice as much food as usual, measuring two omers for each person. The leaders of the community noticed the double portion and hurried to report it to Moses. They were surprised and wanted to understand why this day yielded so much.

Moses explained that the next day was to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath set apart for the Lord. He told them to bake or boil what they wished for the sixth day and set aside the leftover food for the next morning. This was the first explicit rule about resting on the seventh day given in the book of Exodus.

differ.view: The Sabbath was an ancient law given at creation and known by the patriarchs, which God was now renewing after Israel's long slavery in Egypt.
The Sabbath was not yet a practiced law for Israel, and this event was God's first introduction of the weekly rest to the nation before Sinai.

notes.meaning: The people kept the remaining food until the next morning just as Moses had directed. Unlike on other days, the food stayed fresh, did not stink, and had no maggots in it. God miraculously kept the food clean so His people could enjoy their day of rest.

Moses told the people to eat the saved food because the seventh day was a holy Sabbath to the Lord. He warned them that for six days they could gather, but on the seventh day no food would fall on the ground. God removed the daily labor so they could focus on resting with Him.

Even after clear warnings, some of the people went out into the fields on the seventh day to search for food. They searched the ground but found nothing at all. Their lack of trust led to wasted effort because God's word proved entirely true.

The Lord spoke to Moses and asked how long the people would refuse to obey His commandments and teachings. Despite all the signs they had seen, some still chose their own way over God's commands. God showed that ignoring His rules for rest was a serious act of disobedience.

Moses reminded the people that the Sabbath was a gift of rest from the Lord, which is why God gave two days' worth of bread on the sixth day. He commanded everyone to stay in their tents and not wander out searching for food. Hearing this, the people finally obeyed and rested on the seventh day.

The family of Israel named this bread manna, a name that came from asking what it was. It looked like small white coriander seeds and had a sweet taste like flat wafers made with honey. God provided a food that was not only nourishing, but also pleasant to eat.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern writers have suggested manna was the sweet gum that drops from tamarisk shrubs in the Sinai peninsula, but commentators point out that natural gum cannot be baked or ground into flour and never appears in amounts large enough to feed a nation.

notes.meaning: Moses shared God's command to save an omer of manna for future generations. God wanted future children to see the exact bread He provided in the wilderness when He brought their ancestors out of Egypt. Remembering God's past care strengthens faith for the future.

Moses told Aaron to take a jar, fill it with an omer of manna, and place it before the Lord to be kept safe. This jar was preserved so that future generations could witness the miracle. The manna inside was kept from spoiling as a lasting sign of God's power.

Aaron placed the jar in front of the Testimony, meaning beside the ark containing the stone tablets of the law. This sacred placement occurred once the tabernacle and its sacred chest were built. It served as a permanent reminder that the God who gives His law also feeds His people.

The Israelites ate manna for forty full years until they arrived at an inhabited land. This daily gift continued without fail until they reached the border of Canaan, the promised land. God's miraculous care never stopped during their long wilderness journey.

The chapter closes with an explanatory note stating that an omer is one tenth of an ephah. This ancient dry measure amounted to roughly two to three quarts. It helped later readers understand the generous daily portion God provided for every single person.
